use_credential.description: Report that a credential was used, for the keypads and door controllers Lock Code Manager cannot watch itself. The response says whether the code would work, for which user, and the reason when it would not. A valid code fires the Lock Code Manager credential used event; an invalid one fires nothing, so react to a rejection from the response. It touches no lock and changes nothing. It performs no rate limiting and no logging, and the reason tells a real credential that is merely inactive apart from one that is unknown, so do not expose it to untrusted input.

lock_setup_failed.description:

Its entities are created but unavailable, and code synchronization is paused for this lock. After addressing the cause, reload the lock's integration (or Lock Code Manager) to retry. This issue will be automatically dismissed when setup succeeds.

lock_dropped.description:

No entities were created for that lock and no codes are written to it; every other lock in the entry is unaffected. This usually means the entity belongs to a bridge no Lock Code Manager provider supports, or that its integration has changed what it publishes about the device. Remove it from the entry, or fix the underlying cause and reload Lock Code Manager. This issue will be automatically dismissed once the lock sets up.

lock_re_paired_work_dropped.title: Lock Code Manager: check slots {slots} on re-paired {lock_entity_id}

init.title: Check slots {slots} on re-paired {lock_entity_id}
init.description:
`{lock_entity_id}` was re-paired, so Home Assistant now sees it as a different device. Lock Code Manager was still clearing a code from, or writing a one-off PIN to, slots {slots} on the old device. That work was dropped with the old device.

If this is the same physical lock (for example, moved to another Zigbee integration, or re-joined after Home Assistant removed it), a removed user's code may still be in those slots and may still open the door. Check those slots on the lock, and clear any code that shouldn't be there: from the Lock Code Manager card, the unmanaged-code repairs, or the lock itself.

Lock Code Manager does not clear them on its own: on a new device, those slots may hold codes set at its keypad.

Click **Submit** to acknowledge this issue.

lock_re_paired_reload.title: Reload Lock Code Manager to use re-paired {lock_entity_id}
lock_re_paired_reload.description:
`{lock_entity_id}` was re-paired, so Home Assistant now sees it as a different device. A read of the lock was still going when Lock Code Manager switched over, so it is still using the old device, and codes are not synchronized to the new one.

Reload Lock Code Manager to use the new device. This issue will be automatically dismissed when it does.

init.title: Unmanaged code on {lock} in slot {slot}
init.description:
Lock {lock} has a code programmed in slot {slot}, and no Lock Code Manager configuration accounts for it.

There are two ways this happens, and Lock Code Manager cannot tell them apart:

- Somebody programmed the code directly on the lock's keypad or in another app.
- Lock Code Manager left it behind. Before this version, deleting a user removed them from the configuration without clearing their code from the lock, so codes stranded that way are still there and still work.

Until this is settled, slot {slot} stays out of use: Lock Code Manager will not assign a new user to a slot it can still read a code in, because overwriting somebody's own code is the worse mistake.

**Clear the code** removes it from the lock. It stops working immediately and cannot be recovered — choose this only if you know nobody relies on it.

**Keep the code** leaves it exactly as it is and stops asking about this slot.
